paragraphs: David wanted to do something kind, and it blew up in his face. He said, "I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me," and he sent servants to console Hanun (2 Samuel 10:2). Hanun's princes asked whether David was really there to "explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it" (2 Samuel 10:3). Friend, I know that move. You mean well, somebody whispers in the ear, and now your good deed gets a whole different reading.

Kindness doesn't come with a guarantee that people will receive it well. David's servants were thoroughly humiliated for it, and I think that one hurt (2 Samuel 10:4-5). But look at what David does next. He looks after his men first, telling them to stay in Jericho until their beards grew back (2 Samuel 10:5). A good leader covers his people before he does anything else.

Then comes the battle, and Joab shows us how to face a fight you can't dodge. He plans with his brother, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, then you will come to my rescue," and he says, "Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight" (2 Samuel 10:11-12). Give it everything you've got, and leave the outcome with the LORD. In the end the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore (2 Samuel 10:19), so you can do right, take the hit, stay faithful, and still trust God with the rest.
